summary: Mexico and the US completed a third round of US-Mexico-Canada Agreement review talks, deferring tariffs and rules of origin to a fourth round in Washington in September. Separately, the US reopened its border to Mexican cattle imports after a year-long ban meant to contain American beef prices, while Mexico's statistics agency reported Mexico lost more than 500,000 industrial jobs in June, with services also posting sharp losses despite the World Cup.

lead.h1: Mexico and US set fourth round of talks to review the US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement for September
lead.context: Mexico and the US finished a third round of trade negotiations but left tariffs and rules of origin for a fourth round in Washington in September.
lead.background: The United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement is in its first joint review. Washington declined a 16-year extension, so the agreement remains in force but can return to annual reviews while disagreements remain unresolved.
lead.view: The agreement is not about to disappear. The cost is uncertainty. Existing factories can keep shipping, but a company considering a long-payback plant has to assume the rules may be negotiated again next year.
lead.prediction: Expect another progress statement in September rather than a final agreement on tariffs or rules of origin. A specific tariff schedule or revised rules of origin would be evidence that the talks have moved beyond general commitments. Until then, companies considering long-payback investments still have to assume the rules may change again next year.
lead.drivers: Work aims to strengthen North American economic security and competitiveness through deeper supply-chain integration, as Washington pushes to cut reliance on Asian suppliers.
lead.implications: The talks proceeded even as the US formalized a 10% tariff on Mexican goods tied to forced labor.
lead.next: A fourth round covering tariffs and rules of origin is set for Washington in September.

items.headline: Mexico loses more than 500,000 industrial jobs in June
items.context: The services sector also reported sharp job losses despite the World Cup, adding to signs of a weakening labor market this year.
items.background: Mexico's National Occupation and Employment Survey (national labor survey), run by Mexico's statistics agency, tracks month-to-month changes in formal and informal employment across sectors including manufacturing, construction, mining and services.
items.view: A monthly drop of 611,978 industrial jobs, with manufacturing accounting for 482,652 of that and construction another 120,877, is a sharp reversal for an economy already growing near 0.6% in 2025 with fixed investment falling from 23.8% to 22.4% of gross domestic product. The construction losses matter most for nearshoring claims, because physical construction, not investment announcements, is the actual evidence that new plants are being built. Services losing 597,891 jobs the same month, despite World Cup-driven demand, suggests the weakness is broad rather than sector-specific.
items.prediction: Further national labor survey readings are likely to show continued softness in manufacturing and construction employment unless fixed investment as a share of gross domestic product stops declining. That view would be wrong if the next national labor survey release shows industrial employment rebounding without a matching jump in fixed investment or grid connections.

items.headline: United States reopens border to Mexican cattle imports after year-long ban
items.context: The US had blocked Mexican cattle for more than a year to contain rising beef prices for American consumers. The reopening is meant to ease pressure on meat costs while keeping monitoring in place.
items.background: The United States suspended Mexican cattle imports for more than a year after detecting New World screwworm, a parasite that can kill cattle within days, and the ban became entangled with a separate US effort to bring down record domestic beef prices.
items.view: Reopening one port of entry, with two more to follow later, is a phased and partial move, not a full resumption of pre-ban trade. The immediate winners are Mexican cattle exporters near Douglas, Arizona, and US buyers facing high beef prices, but continued screwworm monitoring means the reopening depends on the parasite staying under control rather than on the trade relationship alone.
items.prediction: Cattle shipments through Douglas most likely resume on the stated 30-day timeline, with the New Mexico ports following afterward. That would be wrong if a new screwworm detection forces the US to suspend the reopening before shipments start.

items.headline: Third round of trade agreement review ends with plans for September meeting
items.context: Mexican and US officials completed a third round of technical talks on the US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement and agreed to reconvene in Washington in September, part of the pact's first mandated joint review.
items.background: Under Article 34.7 of the trade agreement, the United States, Mexico and Canada must hold a joint review since Washington declined the option of a 16-year extension on 1 July 2026, and the countries now review the pact annually rather than renegotiating it outright.
items.view: A third round ending in another meeting date, rather than a text or a decision, shows the review is still at the technical-talks stage, not the negotiating stage. Steel, aluminum and Chinese-content rules are being discussed, but nothing here changes rules of origin or tariffs for a single exporter yet. The benefit for now goes to officials who can point to "constructive" progress without committing either government to a position.
items.prediction: The fourth round in September most likely produces further technical alignment rather than a signed change to the agreement's terms. That expectation would be wrong if the September meeting instead produces a joint statement on specific rule changes, such as new steel or automotive content thresholds.
items.drivers: Talks focused on steel, aluminum and derivative products, regional value chains, and reducing reliance on Asian imports, led by Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard and US trade office Jamieson Greer.
items.next: The two governments will hold a fourth round of talks in the first half of September to continue the joint review.
